en: The Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru Receiving the Prediction, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the kingdom of Rājagṛha. At that time...
King Ajātaśatru invited the Buddha, and when the meal was finished, the Buddha returned to the Jetavana.
The King consulted with Jīvaka, saying:
"Today I invited the Buddha, and the Buddha has already finished his meal; what else would be appropriate to do next?"
Jīvaka replied, "It would require many lamps. Thereupon,
the King ordered that a hundred *hù* of sesame oil be prepared, [to be used] from the palace gate to the Jetavana Vihāra.

At that time, there was a poor old woman who always possessed a sincere heart and wished to make offerings to the Buddha, yet lacked the means to do so. Seeing the King performing such meritorious deeds, she was moved to even greater emotion; she went out to beg and obtained two coins, with which she went to an oil merchant's house to buy some oil.
The oil merchant said:
"Your mother is extremely poor; she begged for two coins—why did you not buy food with them to sustain yourself, instead using this oil?"
The mother said, “I have heard that the birth of a Buddha is difficult to encounter, met but once in a hundred kalpas.

Fortunately, I have lived in the age of a Buddha, yet I have been unable to make offerings. Today, seeing the King perform such great merit—so majestic and immeasurable—it has stirred my resolve. Though I am truly poor, I wish to light a single lamp as a foundation for future lives.”

Thereupon, the oil merchant, perceiving her sincere intention, gave her two coins' worth of oil, which should have yielded two *he* (measures); however, he specially increased it by three *he*, so that she received five *he* in total.
Her mother then went forth and lit it before the Buddha.
He calculated that this oil would not last even half a night, and so he made a vow to himself:
"If, in a future life, I attain the Way as a Buddha, may this oil remain bright throughout the entire night without being consumed."
Having paid homage, she departed.
The lamps lit by the king were either extinguished or exhausted; although there were attendants, they could never keep them supplied all around.
Yet the single lamp lit by the old woman shone with extraordinary brilliance, surpassing all the other lamps, remaining unextinguished throughout the night and its oil undiminished.
When morning dawned on the following day, the mother came forward again, prostrated herself with her head at [the Buddha's] feet, and stood back with her hands joined in reverence.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"The night has now turned to day; you may extinguish the lamps."

Maudgalyāyana, having received these instructions, extinguished the lamps one by one in order. When all the lamps had been extinguished, only this mother’s single lamp remained; though he extinguished it three times, it would not go out. He then raised his *kāṣāya* robe to fan it, but the light of the lamp grew even brighter.

He then used his supernormal power to summon the Sūciloma wind to blow upon the lamps in succession, yet the old woman’s lamp became even more intense and fierce, shining upward as far as the Brahma Heaven and sideways across the trichiliocosm, so that its light was seen everywhere.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: “Stop! Stop!”
This radiance and merit of the future Buddha cannot be extinguished by your supernatural power.

This mother, having in her past lives made offerings to eighteen billion Buddhas and received a prophecy from those former Buddhas, devoted herself to teaching and transforming the people through the sutras and the Dharma; she had no leisure to practice *dāna*, and therefore she is now poor and possesses no wealth or treasures.

After thirty kalpas, his merit will be fully perfected and he shall attain Buddhahood, with the title Tathāgata Sumeruprabhāsa, the Arhat. In that world there will be no sun or moon; all people will possess great radiance within their own bodies, and the palaces and mansions, composed of various jewels, will reflect light upon one another like those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Upon hearing this definitive pronouncement, the old woman was filled with joy; she immediately rose lightly into the air to a height of one hundred and eighty *zhang* above the ground, then descended, prostrated herself with her head at his feet, and departed.
When the king heard this, he asked Jīvaka:
"I have performed such magnificent meritorious deeds, yet the Buddha did not grant me a prediction;
yet this mother, by lighting a single lamp, has received a prediction."
"Why is this so? Jīvaka replied, "Though the King has performed many deeds, his mind was not single-minded; it did not focus upon the Buddha as this mother’s heart does."
He then went once more to invite the Buddha.
He had previously instructed the garden supervisors to each gather fine flowers at dawn and bring them early into the palace by midday.
The Buddha then departed from the Jetavana at dawn, walking slowly and steadily while preaching the Dharma to the people along the way, arriving at the palace by midday.

There was a park keeper who, while carrying flowers, happened to come out onto the street of the park and encountered the Buddha on the main road. Hearing the Buddha preach the sutra, he rejoiced with single-minded devotion and immediately scattered all the flowers he was carrying over the Buddha; the flowers remained suspended in mid-air directly above the Buddha’s head.
The Buddha then conferred upon him the prediction, saying:
"You have already made offerings to nine billion buddhas; after one hundred and forty kalpas, you shall become a buddha named Juehua Tathāgata."
The man was filled with joy; he immediately levitated his body and ascended into the void. Having descended and completed his prostrations, he thought again to himself:

"My king is by nature stern and impetuous; he previously commanded me to observe the fast and bring flowers to offer to the Buddha. Yet I have offered them all myself and am now going empty-handed. He will surely put me to death."
He then went straight home, placed the box of empty flowers outside the door, and entered to tell his wife:
"I have not eaten since this morning; the King intends to execute me now, so prepare food for me immediately."
Upon hearing this, the wife was greatly terrified and asked in alarm,
"For what reason would Your Majesty kill me?
He then related the matter to her from beginning to end.
The wife immediately went out and prepared food by the hearth. Śakra, Lord of the Devas, then filled an empty box with celestial flowers.
When the wife returned with the food, she saw that the box outside the door was as full of flowers as before, and their radiance was extraordinary; she immediately informed her husband.
The man went out his door and saw that these were heavenly flowers; his heart was filled with great joy, and he stopped eating and took the flowers inside.
Just as he entered, the King happened to come out to welcome the Buddha and encountered him on the way.
The king, seeing that the flower was magnificent and rare in the world, immediately asked the supervisor:
"There are such excellent flowers as these in abundance within my garden, yet you have not presented them to me before or after; your crime deserves death—do you realize this or not?"
The superintendent said,
"Great King! There are no such flowers in the garden."

Early this morning, as I was carrying garden flowers along the road, I encountered the Buddha. Overcome with joy, I offered them all to him, and he immediately bestowed upon me a prophecy of my future attainment.
Knowing that I was about to be put to death, I returned home to seek food; when I came out to look at the empty box a short while later, I saw these flowers there once again.
"This must be celestial flowers; they do not belong to this garden.

Now that my birth is so lowly and base—I serve as a king's gardener, constrained by the local officials such that I cannot practice the Way—once I have received this prediction and die right now, I shall surely be reborn in the heavens.
There, before the Buddhas of the ten directions, I will be free from all constraints and able to practice the Way at will."
"If the King were to kill me, I would have nowhere to go.

Upon hearing this prediction of his future destiny, the King was immediately struck with shame and fear; his hair stood on end in solemn awe, and he rose at once to prostrate himself, kneeling long before him to repent.
When the Buddha arrived at the palace and had finished his meal, he offered words of blessing and departed.
The King again asked Jīvaka:
"Previously, when I invited the Buddha, my old mother received her prediction [of enlightenment];"
"Today we have made offerings for merit, and the garden supervisor has received the prediction of his future enlightenment;
why is it that I alone have gained nothing at all?
My heart is deeply distressed; what further meritorious deeds should I perform?"

Jīvaka said, "Although Your Majesty has frequently established meritorious offerings day after day, you have used the wealth of the state treasury and employed the labor of the people; thus, your mind may have become arrogant and your intent may have been prone to anger, which is why you have not yet attained certainty."

"Now you should sacrifice the personal articles for your own use within your body, and remove your necklaces, seven-jeweled beads, and rings to fashion them into jeweled flowers. You should present these to the Queen; then, together with the Crown Prince, you shall join your palms with single-minded diligence and devotion to the Buddha. The Buddha will perceive the King’s utmost sincerity, and you will surely receive his decision."

Thereupon, the king reduced his culinary provisions and observed the fast day and night; he removed all the jewels from his person and gathered the various masters together, saying, "Make flowers as before. The king, the queen, and the prince all took part with their own hands until, after ninety days, everything was completed. He then commanded the outer attendants to prepare the carriage for the journey to the Buddha.
An attendant minister reported, saying:
"We have heard that the Buddha previously arrived in the kingdom of Kuśinagara and has already entered parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing this, the king’s heart was filled with great sorrow; he wailed aloud, his voice choked with tears as he said:

"I have therefore made these flowers with my own hands from the depths of my heart; although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, I shall nevertheless carry them to Vulture Peak Mountain to place them upon the Buddha’s seat, thereby expressing my devotion."
Jīvaka said: “The Buddha has no body and there is no nirvana; he neither abides eternally nor is he subject to extinction or location.
Only those with the utmost sincerity can behold the Buddha; though the Buddha dwells in the world, those who lack such sincerity do not see him.”
"Great King, since your sincerity is such, although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, you will surely see him if you go.

He then proceeded to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; seeing the Buddha, he was both sorrowful and joyful. Weeping as he advanced, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and scattered seven-jeweled flowers before him. The flowers all remained suspended in mid-air, transforming into a precious canopy directly above the Buddha.

The Buddha then conferred upon the king a prediction of enlightenment, saying: "Eighty thousand kalpas hence, in an eon named *Priyadarśana*, you shall become a Buddha. Your Buddha-name shall be *Viśuddhamaṇḍala* Tathāgata, your buddha-field shall be named *Puṣparāja*, and at that time the lifespan of the people shall be forty minor kalpas."

The Crown Prince of King Ajātaśatru, named Jñānagupta, was then eight years old. Seeing his father receive this prediction of enlightenment, he was filled with great joy. He immediately removed the various jewels from his person and scattered them over the Buddha, saying:

"I vow that when you purify your realm and attain Buddhahood, I shall become a Golden-Wheel Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) to make offerings to you. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, I shall succeed you as a Buddha."
The jewels he scattered transformed into a jeweled canopy that perfectly covered the Buddha above him.

The Buddha said: "Your wish shall surely be fulfilled. When you become a Buddha, you will first be a Golden-Wheel Universal Monarch (Cakravartin). At the end of your life, you will ascend to be born in Tuṣita Heaven; when your celestial lifespan there ends, you will descend to become a Buddha in the land of Bhaiṣajyarāja, where you will teach and transform beings. Your Buddha-name shall be Candana. The lifespan of the people and all the features of your land shall be exactly like those of the realm of Śuddhāvāsa."

When the Buddha had finished bestowing the prophecy, King Ajātaśatru and Caṇḍa-Andhala came forward and prostrated before the Buddha; immediately, they were suddenly unable to see where the Buddha was.
*The Sūtra on the Prophecy Bestowed upon King Ajātaśatru*
